did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title identifies it as a Miktam of David and emphasizes that it was also intended for instruction: “A Miktam of David, for teaching.”
The psalm mentions conflicts with Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah, and Edom. According to the text, Joab returned from the campaign and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, where twelve thousand fell.
At the beginning of the psalm proper, a national crisis is described in intense language: a sense of abandonment, devastation, divine anger, and the need for God’s restoration.
The land is described as though it had trembled and split apart, and the speaker asks God to heal its fractures because it is collapsing.
The trouble is compared to poisonous wine: the people describe their hardship as a drink they were given that caused them turmoil and suffering.
Alongside the description of the crisis comes hope: God gives a banner to those who fear him, a sign or standard under which they may rally and find protection.
The speaker asks for deliverance for “your beloved ones” and makes a twofold request to God: save them by your right hand and answer the prayer.
The verse presents God as speaking in his holiness and then mentions Shechem and the Valley of Succoth as parts of the land to be divided and measured.
Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah are listed together; within the psalm, they represent different regions and tribes united under the speaker’s leadership.
Moab, Edom, and Philistia are portrayed through images of humiliation and domination: Moab is “my washbasin,” a shoe is thrown over Edom, and a challenge is directed at Philistia.
The conclusion emphasizes the people’s dependence on God: human deliverance is described as futile, but with God’s help they can achieve victory, and he is the one who will trample their enemies.
